From Zohran Mamdani to Abdul El-Sayed—US voters are challenging Trump’s identity politics

US midterm election has also brought attention to something that once seemed almost unthinkable in US politics. The Left and Right are beginning to question the same policies.

Amana Begam

06 November, 2026 10:16 am IST

U S elections have never been just about American voters. The people who cast their votes may be Americans, but the consequences of their choices are often felt across the world.

And this time, the world seems to be watching with even greater interest. Driven by escalating wars, shifting global alliances, and growing cultural divisions, American politics now serves as a critical barometer—not only for the nation’s internal future but also for the trajectory of the wider world.

There is no doubt that people across the world are watching the US midterm election closely, many feeling that their own future, or even the future of the world, may depend on its outcome. Wherever you look, people are discussing the results, analysing what they mean and wondering what comes next. Few elections in the world attract this kind of attention beyond their own borders.

Show Full Article

Beyond culture wars The election results are clear, and to be fair, they are not entirely surprising. US President Donald Trump returned to power with big promises about the economy, ending wars and using tariffs to make America stronger. But many voters do not seem happy with what they have seen so far.

Look at what voters themselves are saying.

According to an election-day survey conducted by SSRS , 39 per cent of voters said the economy was the most important issue, followed by 32 per cent who chose the state of democracy. Nearly 65 per cent believed Trump’s policies had made the economy worse, while 79 per cent said inflation had caused their families severe or moderate hardship.

And it was not just the economy. Around 62 per cent believed the US had made the wrong decision to take military action against Iran.

What I find interesting about these results and surveys is that people seem to have voted based on their everyday concerns and the problems affecting their lives. All the culture wars we have been watching on social media seem to have become background noise, and it now seems to be over.

It does not look like voters were particularly impressed by images of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detaining immigrants or by tougher restrictions on H-1B visas. These issues may dominate social media discussions, but when people are struggling to pay their bills and worrying about their future, perhaps those cultural battles are not as important to them as they appear online.

Take the example of Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan.

During the election campaign, Trump called El-Sayed a “jihadist” and accused him of having links to the Muslim Brotherhood, without providing evidence to support those claims.

The president of the US was using such language against a Muslim candidate running for public office. The idea was to focus on his Muslim identity, perhaps hoping that associating a Muslim politician with extremism would be enough to discredit him. For years, we have seen how religion, race and immigration have been used to fuel cultural divisions in American politics.

But it did not work. El-Sayed’s victory suggests that these cultural attacks have their limits or are simply losing their impact. Voters were willing to look beyond his religious identity and consider his political ideas.

And there is another interesting aspect to his victory. El-Sayed is openly Muslim but he emphasises more on his progressive economic policies, including universal healthcare.

And El-Sayed’s victory becomes even more interesting when we look at the political obstacles he faced. He had to compete against powerful figures within the Democratic Party, overcome opposition from pro-Israel political groups and eventually defeat the Republicans. In doing so, he also made history as the first Muslim elected to the US Senate.

Also read: Narendra Modi isn’t Donald Trump. India’s electoral math makes it harder to humble BJP

Changing political fault lines Before El-Sayed, there was New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani. His victory as a democratic socialist in one of the world’s most important centres of capitalism had already attracted attention. But many saw it as something that could happen only in a progressive city like New York.

Michigan tells a different story.

Unlike New York City, Michigan is a swing state where neither Democrats nor Republicans can take victory for granted. El-Sayed’s success suggests that progressive economic ideas may have an audience beyond America’s traditionally liberal cities.

The Democratic Party is becoming a place where different identities and political ideas are finding representation. From the first Muslim senator to politicians advocating democratic socialist ideas, the party seems to be bringing together people from very different backgrounds.

We also saw historic victories involving the first Black female governor, the first openly gay male senator and the first female Native American governor. Jewish politicians, too, continue to hold an important place within the party.

This election has also brought attention to something that once seemed almost unthinkable in American politics. On the issue of Israel, parts of the American L eft and R ight are beginning to question the same policies, although for very different reasons.

Politicians like Mamdani and El-Sayed have been critical of Israeli government policies, particularly over the treatment of Palestinians. Their criticism comes from a progressive political perspective, focused on human rights, equality and opposition to war.

But interestingly, criticism of American support for Israel is also coming from sections of the right, including parts of the MAGA movement . Their concerns are different. They question why American taxpayers’ money should be spent supporting another country when Americans themselves are struggling with economic problems. For them, it is a question of putting America first.

Of course, this does not mean the L eft and R ight ideologues suddenly agree on Israel or on foreign policy. Their reasons for questioning American support are often very different, and many Republicans remain strong supporters of Israel.

There is something El-Sayed said in his victory speech that I think goes beyond American politics.

He reminded people that America is big enough for everyone, regardless of what they look like or how they pray.

And I think humanity will truly move forward when this becomes a reality not just in America, but in every part of the world, regardless of who lives there, what they believe or how they choose to live; they belong.

Because in the end, shouldn’t that be the vision of every society?

Amana Begam Ansari is a columnist, writer, and TV news panellist. She runs a weekly YouTube show called ‘India This Week by Amana and Khalid’. She tweets @Amana_Ansari. Views are personal.

(Edited by Saptak Datta)

Nov 5 (Reuters) – Ukraine must adapt to the new realities of US politics to build dialogue and address its needs for more foreign aid and bolstered air defences to counter Russian attacks, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said in an interview broadcast on Thursday.

Zelenskiy has made considerable effort to smooth over a volatile relationship with US President Donald Trump, particularly after a February 2025 Oval Office meeting during which he was accused of being ungrateful for Washington’s aid.

US-led talks with Ukraine and Russia on resolving the conflict are scheduled to resume next week in Abu Dhabi.

Show Full Article

Zelenskiy, attending an Ibero-American summit in Spain, told Ukrainian television channel TSN that Kyiv had to adapt to a changed US political landscape after voters in US midterm elections put Democrats in control of Congress.

“Ukraine has to move forward towards the new political infrastructure in the United States of America,” he said.

“We have to move quickly. Without doubt, we have to unite the bipartisan support that we get. Understanding the power shifts, we should build up our dialogue the right way. I believe we have the chance to increase support.”

Ukraine needs to become stronger through aid packages and recover what he described as $16 billion in assistance that he said Washington promised but did not deliver.

PATRIOT MISSILES TOP PRIORITY

The country’s main priority, he said, was enhancing air defences as the war against Russia extends past the 4-1/2-year mark. That meant ensuring supplies of missiles for the US Patriot air defence system.

“If we don’t solve the Patriot problem, it will get very tough for us,” he said. “This issue could be solved by Europe, some countries outside Europe and, of course, the United States of America. This is the No. 1 priority.”

The US State Department said last week it had approved the sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles to Ukraine for an estimated $2.1 billion. The missiles are not expected to be delivered until the early 2030s, however.

Zelenskiy said he was also working to ensure Ukraine has enough operating F-16 fighter jets over the next five to six months.

Ukraine is facing another winter of Russian strikes on its energy sector, with the situation in the capital Kyiv being “the most difficult,” he said.

Zelenskiy said EU, NATO and US officials, meeting this week in Brussels, were working out proposals for security guarantees at the end of the conflict and making some progress. US envoy Jared Kushner, writing on X, called the talks productive and substantive.

(Reporting by Ron Popeski and Bogdan Kochubey; Editing by Rod Nickel)

Two Egyptian army officers killed in gold-mining crackdown on southern border, military says

CAIRO, Nov 5 (Reuters) – Two Egyptian army officers, including a high-ranking border guard officer, were killed during a military crackdown on illegal gold mining along Egypt’s southern border with Sudan, a military spokesperson said on Thursday.

The military launched the campaign to counter illegal gold mining in the Eastern Desert in June, with the first three phases complete.  The military said the fourth phase was due to begin on Saturday, adding the campaign intended to strengthen state control over Egyptian territory and protect national resources.

It was not immediately clear when the two officers were killed, and the spokesperson did not specify the timing of their deaths.

Show Full Article

The military spokesperson said authorities had detained 151 Egyptians and 540 foreigners during the campaign.

The campaign has drawn attention after the rights monitor Emergency Lawyers said in October that at least 72 artisanal miners had been killed in an airstrike in northern Sudan, close to the Egyptian border. The group blamed the Egyptian Air Force for the strike.

Egypt’s military did not refer to the reported strike or the deaths at the time. In a statement then, it said a phase of its campaign against illegal gold mining in southern Egypt was under way after it dropped warning leaflets on what it described as “criminal elements.”

Artisanal gold mining has risen in northern Sudan since Sudan’s civil war disrupted livelihoods. Gold has become a key revenue source during the conflict, while experts and industry participants say much of it is smuggled into Egypt through a porous and disputed border area that includes the mineral-rich Halayeb and Shalateen regions.

The Egyptian military spokesperson said there was coordination with Sudan, including recent meetings between Egyptian and Sudanese officials. He said the armed forces of both countries exchanged information on securing the Egypt-Sudan border.

(Reporting by Ali Khafagi, Nayera Abdallah, Hatem Maher, Enas Alashray and Yomna Ehab; Writing by Enas Alashray; Editing by Chris Reese and Rod Nickel)
